column1: How does a trigger's execution differ from an ordinary stored-procedure call?
column2:
A trigger runs automatically in response to its specified event.
Application code does not explicitly call it like an ordinary stored procedure.
Review source

column1: Which trigger category responds to INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statements on a table or view?
column2:
A DML trigger.
DML means data manipulation language.
Review source

column1: Which trigger category responds to schema events such as CREATE, ALTER, or DROP?
column2:
A DDL trigger.
DDL means data definition language.
Review source

column1: When does an AFTER DML trigger run?
column2:
After the statement's actions and constraint checks succeed.
AFTER does not mean after the enclosing transaction commits.
Review source

column1: What does an INSTEAD OF trigger do to the original modification?
column2:
It replaces the original operation with the trigger's logic.
The trigger must implement any required changes to the underlying data.
Review source

column1: Which DML trigger timing supports triggers on views?
column2:
INSTEAD OF.
SQL Server does not support AFTER triggers on views.
Review source

column1: Which logical trigger table contains new row versions for INSERT or UPDATE?
column2:
inserted.
SQL Server creates and manages this table for the triggering statement.
Review source

column1: Which logical trigger table contains old row versions for DELETE or UPDATE?
column2:
deleted.
For UPDATE, it holds the values from before the modification.
Review source

column1: For an unchanged ProductID primary key, how can an UPDATE trigger pair old and new rows?
column2:
Join inserted and deleted on ProductID.
Do not rely on row position to match the versions.
Review source

column1: How many times does each matching INSERT trigger fire for one 100-row INSERT statement?
column2:
Once for the statement.
Its inserted table contains all 100 rows, rather than one row per invocation.
Review source

column1: What coding style handles multiple affected rows in a DML trigger?
column2:
Set-based logic that processes every affected row.
Do not assume that inserted or deleted contains only one row.
Review source

column1: How must an inventory trigger handle several inserted order lines for the same ProductID?
column2:
Aggregate SUM(Quantity) by ProductID before subtracting each total.
UPDATE...FROM does not automatically sum duplicate matches in inserted.
Review source

column1: What does UPDATE(Price) tell a trigger?
column2:
An INSERT or UPDATE attempt targeted Price.
It does not prove that the stored value changed.
Review source

column1: What does d.Price <> i.Price evaluate to when exactly one price is NULL?
column2:
UNKNOWN.
A WHERE clause therefore misses that NULL-to-value or value-to-NULL change.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2022 and later, which predicate detects nullable Price changes between deleted d and inserted i?
column2:
d.Price IS DISTINCT FROM i.Price.
NULL-to-value and value-to-NULL transitions count as changes.
Review source

column1: How can one DML trigger respond to multiple modification events?
column2:
List the events, separated by commas, in its definition.
Example: AFTER INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
Review source

column1: When is combining several DML events into one trigger appropriate?
column2:
When those events share the required trigger logic.
Separate triggers can keep different per-event logic easier to maintain.
Review source

column1: Why must DML trigger code stay short and efficient?
column2:
It adds synchronous work to the firing transaction.
A long-running trigger can prolong resource locks and increase blocking.
Review source

column1: How can a trigger defer expensive follow-up processing?
column2:
Write an event to a queue table for a separate worker.
Keep the queue insert transactional and perform the slow work outside the trigger.
Review source

column1: What is direct recursion of an AFTER trigger?
column2:
The trigger's own modification causes that same trigger to fire again.
Repeated self-triggering can form a loop.
Review source

column1: Which database option controls direct recursion of AFTER triggers?
column2:
RECURSIVE_TRIGGERS.
Setting it to OFF prevents direct recursion of AFTER triggers.
Review source

column1: Why does RECURSIVE_TRIGGERS OFF not prevent every trigger loop?
column2:
It only prevents direct recursion of AFTER triggers.
Indirect trigger chains need separate controls and careful trigger design.
Review source

column1: Which transaction contains a DML trigger's changes?
column2:
The same transaction as the statement that fired it.
An error can affect the whole transaction, depending on its type and handling.
Review source

column1: Which statement raises a custom validation error from a trigger?
column2:
THROW.
Example: THROW 50001, 'Order date cannot be in the future', 1;
Review source

column1: Why must trigger behavior be documented for other developers?
column2:
Triggers can cause changes that are invisible in application code.
Document the triggering events and the purpose of the resulting actions.
Review source

column1: Why must DML trigger code tolerate empty inserted and deleted tables?
column2:
A valid triggering statement can affect zero rows.
An early return can avoid unnecessary work for such a statement.
Review source
